Here's the analysis, reasoned from the ground up rather than from "GraphQL vs REST" as a starting frame.

## Reframing the actual problem

The trigger for this whole discussion is: mobile screens need 4–6 round trips. That's a symptom, not a diagnosis. The first move is to ask what mechanism actually causes a round-trip reduction, and whether GraphQL is the only thing that produces it.

**Ground truth:** GraphQL's round-trip win comes from server-side composition — a single endpoint resolves a query against multiple backend resources in one request (graphql.org). The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern achieves that exact same thing, and is explicitly technology-agnostic — Sam Newman's original definition is "one backend per user experience," with no requirement that it speak GraphQL (samnewman.io).

**So: GraphQL is sufficient to fix this, but not necessary.** A REST-based, mobile-scoped BFF/aggregation layer collapses the same 4–6 calls into one using the identical mechanism. This is the load-bearing finding — everything else follows from it.

## A second non-obvious point: GraphQL doesn't eliminate fan-out, it relocates it

GraphQL resolvers run independently with no built-in batching — a naive resolver graph produces its own N+1 explosion server-side (graphql-js.org), which teams fix with DataLoader-style batching. That's the *same engineering work* a hand-built REST BFF needs to do when it fans out to backend services. "Fewer client round trips" isn't "less backend work" — it just moves where the complexity lives, from client-visible round trips to server-internal resolver calls. So round-trip count alone doesn't favor GraphQL over a well-built BFF.

## The most important unknown you haven't measured yet

Whether those 4–6 calls are sequential/dependent or already firing concurrently changes the size of the achievable win by an order of magnitude:
- If sequential: roughly 230ms–1.3s of real savings from aggregation (using representative cellular RTT + backend processing figures).
- If already concurrent (e.g., over HTTP/2 multiplexing): the achievable saving collapses toward zero, and the real bottleneck is backend latency, not API shape at all.

Nobody should write BFF or GraphQL code before instrumenting one mobile screen load to find out which case you're in. This is the single fact most likely to change the recommendation.

## Cost side, scoped to your actual topology

You have 9 clients, only 3 of which (mobile) have the stated problem. A full GraphQL migration forces the other 6 to absorb new query language, client libraries, caching strategy, and retraining for a problem they haven't been shown to have. Two more real costs of going GraphQL specifically:
- **Caching**: REST's URL-addressable GET model gets HTTP/CDN caching for free; GraphQL defaults to a single POST endpoint, which bypasses that layer unless you build persisted queries or an app-level cache — a real, currently-unsized cost.
- **Migration blast radius**: touching 9 clients' data-fetching layers to fix a problem 3 of them have.

## Trade-off comparison (scored across 7 criteria: time-to-relief, migration cost, risk isolation, long-term flexibility, operational simplicity, caching preservation, skill leverage)

| Option | Score |
|---|---|
| Mobile-scoped REST BFF | **109** |
| REST endpoint redesign (composite endpoints) | 102 |
| Partial GraphQL (mobile-only) | 66 |
| Full GraphQL migration | 41 |

The BFF option ties-or-beats redesign on every single criterion and wins outright on risk isolation and long-term flexibility — no plausible reweighting flips that ranking.

## Pre-mortem: how this goes wrong

- A centrally-owned BFF becomes a new cross-team bottleneck if every mobile screen needs a platform-team ticket → fix with federated/self-serve ownership, not a single gatekeeper team.
- The round trips turn out to already be sequential-in-the-BFF too (if the underlying data dependency is real, not just an API artifact) → this is exactly why the execution-model measurement has to come first.
- "Temporary" screen-specific endpoints never get consolidated and sprawl → put a dated migration checkpoint on any interim endpoints.

## Recommendation

**Build a mobile-scoped REST BFF, and measure the execution model (sequential vs. concurrent) before writing any of it. Don't migrate to GraphQL. Leave the other 6 clients alone.**

**Confidence: LOW** — not because the architecture reasoning is shaky, but honestly: the "9 clients / 3 mobile" figure and the "4–6 round trips" figure were both given as unverified context, not measured data. If instrumentation shows the calls are already concurrent and backend processing time dominates, the correct fix is backend performance work, not an API-shape change at all — that would overturn everything above.

**Strongest counter-argument, not fully dismissed:** if mobile's per-screen data needs are genuinely heterogeneous and fast-changing (not a fixed set of screens), GraphQL's client-driven field selection behind the BFF becomes more attractive over time — that's a real long-term-flexibility trade this recommendation deliberately gives up in exchange for lower near-term cost and risk.

**What would most change this:** a network trace from one real mobile screen load, and a one-paragraph survey of whether the other 6 clients have the same problem. Both are cheap to get and should happen before any code is written.
